name: PF-06260414

lead: PF-06260414 is an oral SARM from Pfizer, studied for cachexia, which muscle-building readers follow as a lean-mass candidate.

It belongs to the isoquinoline class and is designed to activate androgen receptors preferentially in muscle and bone. A 2016 paper reported tolerability, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic results from single and multiple ascending oral doses in healthy men. Development was discontinued after Phase I, and efficacy was never tested in trials.

paras: It was given orally in a clinical setting. It is not marketed, and no routine for physique use exists.
Only Phase I tolerability data exist. The SARM class is unapproved and banned by WADA, with case reports of liver injury from recreational use.

angle.text: PF-06260414 is Pfizer's oral SARM, studied for cachexia and designed to activate androgen receptors in muscle and bone. Muscle-building readers follow it as a lean-mass candidate. It was safety-tested in healthy men and shelved after Phase I, with no appearance data.

lead: PF-06260414 is an investigational non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the isoquinoline class, developed by Pfizer and investigated for cachexia; development was discontinued after Phase I [1].

A 2016 paper reported tolerability, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic results from single and multiple ascending oral doses in healthy subjects [2]. It has not been tested for appearance or physique outcomes.

paras: Two Phase I registrations exist: a single and multiple ascending dose study in 72 healthy Western and Japanese men started in February 2014 and is listed as completed [3], and a 2015 bioavailability study of a solid-dose formulation was withdrawn [4].

A 2025 systematic review of randomized trials examined SARMs' effects on physical performance and safety across the class [5]. Analytical chemistry papers also cover SARMs, including mass spectrometry and doping control methods for the class [6].

The Phase I study in healthy subjects assessed tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics after single and multiple ascending doses, including a Japanese cohort [2][3]. A follow-up bioavailability study was withdrawn [4]. No efficacy trial has been reported.
